Integrate a Hamiltonian trajectory

Source: R/integrate.R
simp_integrate.Rd

Advance a separable Hamiltonian system H(q, p) = U(q) + K(p), with kinetic energy K(p) = 0.5 p' Minv p where Minv is the inverse mass matrix, using a symplectic splitting integrator. The integrator conserves a nearby (shadow) energy, so the total energy stays bounded over long trajectories instead of drifting.

Usage

simp_integrate(
  q0,
  p0,
  grad_U,
  eps,
  n_steps,
  integrator = "leapfrog",
  mass = NULL,
  trajectory = FALSE,
  U = NULL
)

Arguments

q0

Numeric vector, the starting position.

p0

Numeric vector, the starting momentum, same length as q0.

grad_U

Function mapping a position vector to the gradient of the potential energy U, that is dU/dq. For a target density with log-density lp, the potential is U = -lp and its gradient is -d(lp)/dq.

eps

Positive step size.

n_steps

Number of integrator steps.

integrator

Name of a built-in scheme; see simp_schemes(). Defaults to "leapfrog".

mass

Mass matrix M. NULL (the default) uses the identity; a numeric vector uses a diagonal mass; a matrix uses a dense mass.

trajectory

If TRUE, return the position and momentum at every step. If FALSE (the default), return only the endpoint.

U

Optional function mapping a position to the potential energy U. When supplied, the total energy is recorded along the returned points.

Value

A list with the endpoint q and p. When trajectory = TRUE it also holds q_path and p_path, each a matrix with one row per retained point and one column per coordinate. When U is supplied it holds energy, the total energy at the retained points.

Examples

# A unit isotropic Gaussian target: U(q) = 0.5 q'q, grad_U(q) = q.
grad_U <- function(q) q
out <- simp_integrate(q0 = c(1, 0), p0 = c(0, 1), grad_U = grad_U,
                      eps = 0.1, n_steps = 60, integrator = "yoshida4")
out$q
#> [1]  0.9601592 -0.2794526
